div1.head: Interview with Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger [8/26/2003]

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger at her home in Mission, Kansas. Helen was a home-front worker during World War II working at the De Soto Kansas Munitions Plant during the summers while she was going to college. Her future husband was oversees at that time -- and we'll discuss him here in a little bit. Helen, where did you grow up as a young lady -- as a young girl?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, I grew up in Kansas City, Kansas. It was out of the Argentine District, and then when I was nine years old we moved to the suburbs which at that time was called a little town of Turner, Kansas, and that's where I grew up and went to grade school, the Turner Grade School, the Turner High School, graduated in 1944.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: 1944 from THS.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you have brothers and sisters -- did you have brothers and sisters?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I have two sisters and they were younger than me that went through the Turner Grade School and also high school.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So there were three girls in your family --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Three girls.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- mom and dad.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Mom and dad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay, what did your daddy do for a living?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: My father worked at the Kansas City, Missouri, stockyards, he was a manager there of several of the car rental places and car service and was connected there with the stock exchange.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Is that right?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh, the old stock exchange building there -- down there.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: It's still there.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh, it still is (chuckles).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, you got out of high school in '44 and that very summer then you worked at the De Soto --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: The De Soto.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- munitions plant.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes -- uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What did you do that summer -- what kind of work did you do?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay. Well, at that time I walked a mile and-a-half to catch the old bus that went out there and I was put on the -- what we called the big presses at that time, it was making machine gun pellets and running these huge big presses.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Now, when you say machine gun pellets, what --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: This was made up of ether and highly flammable, you know, materials, of course, and we run these presses, it was kind of like spaghetti, you know, and we had to be very careful, well-trained on when to cut them off and that sort of thing, to not create a fire.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you actually make the bullets themselves there?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, no, those were transferred out and made -- you know, compressed and shipped out. And then --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were the bullets made at De Soto or did you make only the components for the bullets?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: We only made the components for those and shipped them out, uh-huh, at that time. And then this line kind of cut down or they moved us, they -- supplies, to another line which was called the rocket powder line and this were making the black rocket powder in rolls, big rolls, and those, of course, were made into, you know, for --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: They were shells?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. When you say in rolls --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, we would throw -- we would put the raw powder on the rollers, they were big rollers, and we would have to learn to walk in and back out backwards and wear spacesuit type of things and with the helmets and all. It was very, very dangerous work because it was pure nitroglycerin, a lot of it was, you know, that was made up of the basics and we had a lot of, you know, possible fire, which we did have some, but, you know, we were all trained on how to handle ourselves during that. But we -- it was part -- I mean, it just ran 24 hours a day, I mean, we worked long hours and had to --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How long a shift did you work, an eight-hour shift?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, yes, we had three different shifts around the clock and we all had to rotate, you know, from the morning shifts to the night shifts every few weeks. So, it was kind of a challenge in our lives, especially adjusting from one part of our city or, you know, from one part of our hours day and night, and, of course, getting used to one and then having to jump back was something too, was a little challenge.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you live with your mom and dad?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I lived with my folks and I had to travel from Turner, Kansas on an old bus that the government gave -- you know, provided for us. I had to walk a mile and-a-half each day to catch the bus and home at night and, of course, during the --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Because it was quite a -- maybe 25 miles or something like that.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes -- oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, what time did you have to leave home in the morning to catch the bus if you worked the day shift?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, we had to leave fairly early, about 6 o'clock in the morning because we had, you know, the bus only -- we only had one bus and if you missed it, you were in bad shape so -- and then, of course, in the middle of the night and the all-night buses that, you know, when we were working those shifts. My father sometimes would try to, you know, come and get me because there was hardly any town between that and on the other side of the Santa Fe railroad tracks which I had to walk to, to a little place there that was kind of like a semi-hotel to catch the -- that was used as a bus stop.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh. So you worked the day shift and the night shift --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: The night shift and the afternoon shift.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: The second shift.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh, three shifts.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, actually, if you had to walk an hour -- a mile-and-a-half, rather, to get to the bus and then a mile-and-a-half home --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh, it was --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you have any company there? I mean, for a young lady back in those days it was different, I know --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- but for a young lady alone to be going at 3:00 in the morning --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: That's right, absolutely, and I was by myself and I wasn't afraid. I mean, I just, you know, didn't have -- I guess I was just young and spunky enough that I just felt, you know, it was part of my duty and just never thought about it except that I knew that I would make it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So if you left at 6:00 in the morning, took awhile to get over there and awhile to get home --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- walking. What time would get home usually?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, the bus, we'd have to catch that bus which would bring us back probably around 5:00/6:00 at night because, you know, we --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then you had another forty-five minute walk home --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- had another forty-five minute walk, sure, because we were -- it was a lengthy thing but we never thought about it, I mean, I never thought of --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, for one thing it probably paid better than any other service job you could have; didn't it?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, it certainly did, and that was one reason why we all felt that it -- that's one reason why we all thought that we would like to be on the black rock -- rocket powder because it was the most dangerous and, of course, it paid a little more. But in those days still, you know, still in all, you know, women were paid very little, I mean, you know, according to things, but it did pay --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did they pay the men more than they did the women?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, what few men there were, yes, naturally.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, roughly how many people worked your shift? Any idea? You didn't count them, but how many people?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, I'd say on the shift that I was on and the group that I worked in, I would say there was at least 40 of us.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And that was just a small part --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: All they were women.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- of the protection of the plant.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes -- oh, yes, because it was huge -- it was huge and this was just one part of the plant.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did we have hundreds working there as a __--

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- or thousands maybe?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes -- yes. They had barracks up that some of the people that came in from all parts of Missouri, Kansas, and around had to live there, you know, had to rent, rent little rooms in those barracks and things. So, a lot of the people --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, was there a restaurant then where those people could eat or a chow hall of some kind?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: They had a mess hall, yes, more or less for them. I mean, they had surrounding little places but we had to usually carry our lunches and then we had this -- what we call -- a little wagon that would come around for sandwiches and lunches and stuff like that that they would bring in, the catering -- little catering, and that's the only way we had, you know, other than what we --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Was it hard work physically?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Physically it was not too hard of work, except it was technical and very dangerous, I mean, you know, we had to be on our toes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Who supervised the work? Were there military people supervising the work or civilian men?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: There were some -- very, very few men there but mostly the women but they were -- yes, that we were supervised by. But there was also women that were supervisors that had worked in the government.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, of your 40 people in your department, if you will, on that shift --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- how many of them were men, typically?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, gee, there wasn't over three.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And they were older men or 4-F men, I suppose.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yeah, 4-F, there was a couple -- there was 4-F. We even had a few that came up from down south, I think either Arkansas or one of the southern states, and they were 4-F and some of them were even, you know, semi-illiterate but, you know, it was -- and I don't mean that dismeaningfully, but, you know, they did have -- give them work and, I mean, they did work, but most of us were women and grandmothers.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, young girls like your -- you were just a young woman --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes -- yes. I was just a young -- I was just 18.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- just graduated from high school.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Right. And some of them teachers that were in their late 20s and 30s, teachers and students, college students, a lot of college students.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, but you did not make the actual shells there.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, we didn't put them together. We actually made the components and --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And the components were shipped out somewhere?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Shipped out, yes, as far as I know they were or else they were shipped to a different part of the Sunflower Ordnance which could have been into, yes, and those things we were a little unfamiliar with, I mean, you know, we weren't told too much.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Sure, yeah, you were just doing what you did.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: That's right because we had to have quite a bit of security too, you know, there and we weren't allowed to smoke, naturally, and, of course, some of the women would try to smoke in the latrines and everything but if they got caught, they got fired because, you know, it was such a fire hazard.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And, you know, if you've seen a person burned to death, why, it's pretty sad.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did you ever have accidents there, while you were there that you heard?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, I didn't have, I was lucky, I never had a fire but some of my colleagues did, and those kind of fires were the kind that, you know, their flash ___ often and they're so intense that they just take the whole back side of you off, you know, I mean, your clothing and everything.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: H'm.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: So, it was, like I say, it was a very challenging job and we were all naturally, you know, hepped up about the war and we knew that we had to do our doggonedest for it and that we wanted to.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, I mean, the attitude --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Everybody -- the attitude there was go, go, go. If you could move and work, do it for our troops, and we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh -- uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: We really --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, they were working for us so the least we could do was work for them.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: That's right, and we had to -- you know, we figured that they've -- sacrificing their lives so we naturally would --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, there were thousands of people working there and you just saw a piece of it.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes. I was just -- we were just a little -- one little part of it because they were all in different areas and shifts so that it was a very, very large ordnance and a lot of this -- a lot of our firearms and a lot of our fire power came from that plant. It was a big thing.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: It was a big thing. And, of course, your CEOs or some of your fellows, that, you know, were the head fellows there over the plant and things, they even lived there on the land and had their -- the government had built homes for them there.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And I believe there were schools --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, schools and we had a movie house and, you know, things like that for the people that had to live in the area.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh. But you, personally, didn't spend any time other than on the job.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, on the job mostly, because -- yes, because of the back and forth, yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did either of your sisters work out there?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, they were --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Oh, they were quite a bit younger.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- much younger than me, yes -- uh-huh. They were six years and four years younger than me.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. So you got out of high school and you worked there that summer and then what did you do in the fall?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay. In the fall I went to college and I was studying and I was put in with the premedical students at the university.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Where were you studying at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yes. Where?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I was studying -- I think -- let's see, first off I think I was studying there at the junior college.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Kansas City Kansas Junior College.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yeah, Kansas City Kansas Junior College. And then, about a year-and-a-half I went ahead and transferred into KU and then was staying up there. I had to stay there on the campus, of course, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, you worked at the ordnance plant in '54 -- excuse me, '44 --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And '45, and pretty much up there in '46 too. Well, I mostly worked -- by that time I was working up there on the campus of the KU most of the time too.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you graduate KU then?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, yes, I -- we had -- I was in a program there where we had to have one year's internship at the hospital to get our B.S. degree in medical technology and this is where I was in that program so I spent my fifth year there. In 1947 I entered the internship at the hospital for a year.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Was that at KU Medical Center?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, this was not. I didn't take my basic training at KU Medical Center, it was over at Bethany, the Methodist hospital at that time.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh, in Kansas City, Kansas.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And then I took my graduate work all at KU Medical Center and came back and took that and set up the laboratories in the Kansas City area, three labs, and then I worked firstly at -- mostly in the greater Kansas City area Children's Mercy Hospital, the old charitable Children's Mercy Hospital.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And that was quite something because you have to love children to work there. And we -- and then I taught medical students there. I set up the first bacteriology laboratory there. Of course, this was way back there when (chuckles) we didn't have much, you know, it was all either given to us or else -- we didn't even know if we was going to get a paycheck or not, you know, at that time which wasn't that great but at least, you know, it was all dedication. And I'm so glad that I went into it because I was very versatile, I had -- but my graduate work was in bacteriology and microbiology and then later on in the early '60s I went into nuclear medicine. I had a chance when they came into Kansas City.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, you're very well-trained. Let's continue along that line. How long did you work after you got out of school?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay. I worked fifty -- let's see, I was going to say at least 53 years -- 53 or 54 years.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: In the medical field --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: In the medical field after I got out of school, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- retiring when then?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I retired in 1997, I was 70 years old.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: '97, uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You retired.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I believe -- yes, I retired at the -- uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: That was a wonderful career; wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, yes. I was in practically all parts of it too, you know. I became a clinical laboratory II scientist and taught, you know, various parts of the medical profession and then I was, like I say, I just -- and, of course, I felt like I had to take my -- you know, I had to finish my career because I had lost two beautiful children and we had -- I had an Rh factor problem and so I had to work, which I'm glad I had a career at that time.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Let's move back just a little bit. When you worked at the munitions plant you said you had to wear these funny suits, what --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes, they were like -- they were asbestos suits. They were very warm and, of course, you can imagine we had no air conditioning at that time and it was summertime so you -- and then, we wore also the helmets that were -- come completely over our heads and we had the front, you know, you could see through like the space guys look. And then we wore what we called powder shoes which had no nails because of the sparking, you know, any sparks off the powder, off the floor would ignite. And so, we had to change our clothes completely each shift on top of everything else.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Were these suits that you wore, these spaceman suits, were they in case of fire or was there difficulty, you could breathe things that you shouldn't breathe or --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, mostly, and that's why we had to learn to walk backwards when we put stuff on the rollers to burn and, you know, I mean, to season, I should say. We had to learn to walk backwards because in case of fire flashing, it would go out and around us, around our faces and around the helmet, you know, and these came clear down, the asbestos treated, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: But I imagine in the summertime no air conditioning --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, they were pretty rough.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- very, very --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Very hot -- very hot. But we learned to, you know, we just learned to tolerate it because it was just part of our job.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Part of what you had to do.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yes, that's right.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And, you know, times of war and times of disasters, we just do what we can and go on.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: H'm, well, that was terrific. What was the -- if you think about, did you ever have any -- what was the worst day you spent at the powder plant?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Powder plant, okay, yes. When I first transferred to the rocket powder plant rollers, we worked in pure nitroglycerin, like I said to you, and most of us -- this sort of thing gives you extreme high headaches. In other words, you feel like your head's going to blow off and you get just terribly sick. And I never was used to headaches, never had them, you know, unless I knew something was really wrong. And so, I really -- it really hit me, of course, you know, you have to get used to it. They say after you absorb so much that it will, you know, penetrate your body and you will become accustomed to it. So, I was really sick and I had a terrible headache, come home, and said -- my father met me at the door and he said, Helen, what's the matter? And I said, I don't know, Daddy, I've got it at work -- but I says -- I've got to go back. He says, You're not going to go back -- he says -- you're just going to have to quit. I says, Daddy, I have to, I have to complete this so I can finish, you know, going to college. Because I had to work my way through, my folks couldn't afford to send me. So, anyway, he said, Well -- he says -- you're not going to come home like this. And so, some of the grandmothers out there, they were pretty smart. Little old ladies from down south and I really -- you know, we kind of listened to them, some of us youngies, and she said, Now, honey, you've got to tie -- you've got to get some gauze there at the first-aid station and you soak that in vinegar and you wrap your wrist in vinegar -- and she says -- you keep smelling that every time you think you're going to get sick, you just put that up to your nose and smell that -- and she says -- it will subside. And you know, it really worked! It really worked! Just something simple like this and I never would have thought about it, you know. But we all -- I wasn't the only one. There was a lot of us that really got ill from that. But we stuck it out and, of course, we had to be monitored with EKGs, you know, every six weeks or more because of our hearts, you know, it's hard on the heart.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So they'd test you.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I mean, they wanted to be sure you didn't have a heart attack, you know (chuckles). I mean, all sorts of little things that happened (chuckles). Oh, gee, we all lived through it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Part of what you had to do; wasn't it?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: That's right (chuckles).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well -- and you did do it and that was --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, we did it with -- you know, it was just part of the game. And, of course, we had no nylons then. We had to give up nylons. We painted our legs.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Painted the line on your legs?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: We painted our legs to look like nylons, yeah, we (laughing) -- and we had those ol' heavy rayon things, you know, and nobody wanted to wear those. And our panties, we didn't have any rubber in our panties (laughing) so we had --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Draw string?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No (laughing), we had buttons (laughing), which was a bad thing because they could come off (laughing). You could lose your drawers real fast (laughing)! It was something else (laughing)! You didn't realize the rationing until you went out and, you know, you had little stags [ph], little stars, for so many, you know, for gasoline and sugar and flour and stuff like that, you know. We all lived through that (laughing).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Did your daddy -- did your family have a car?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, my father had --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Your daddy took it back and forth to work, probably.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes. He had an old Model A Ford, that's where I learned to drive (laughing). But, yes, and it was a goin' gosslin. He just really -- he was one of the lucky ones, really -- he was one of the lucky ones.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, you met your future -- where did you meet your future husband?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I met him in high school -- in high school, my first year of high school. He came in from another little town outside of Vera Lakes (ph), which was called Holiday, Kansas, and it was an old railroad town, a small one, but it was part of the Santa Fe railway system.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Was he in the same class as you or --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, he was a grade ahead of me.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Grade ahead.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: A grade ahead of me but we were in -- some of our classes, our language, our Latin classes we were together.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Had you started dating at that time?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No. We were just more or less, you know, in a group of kids, you know. In those days we just kind of went in groups and we just -- he was, you know, quite into the activities of the school and same was I. And we were good friends. He was very musical. He could play most instruments, you know, and so we were -- had some common ground there. And then also in theatre and stuff like this and so --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So when he was 18 he must have gotten right out of high school --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, in fact --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and got drafted.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- he was gone the week after he graduated.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: After graduating from high school.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes -- uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, had you talked it over and agreed you was going to write to each other or --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes -- yes, we were going together then.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: I see.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh. And we were fairly serious with one another there, you know, and everything so -- oh, yes, and I faithfully did. We all -- and not just him but, you know, some of the other fellows too because that was the thing that was really, you know, something to get a letter from home no matter, you know, if you were just friends or what.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: No matter who it was from.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: That's right because those guys they were just -- you know, wanting to get anything so they could get their mind off of the war as much as they could, you know, when they were off.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So did -- after some of his training, he probably got a leave and came home and you were a-sparkin' then, were you?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, yes, we were. He had several leaves, yes, and the one -- well, he was shipped right, you know, fairly early right oversees in the 82nd Airborne because that's where it was made up in Brittain, you know, in England there. And, so, he was -- he just had his basic training, you know, maybe six weeks and he had a couple little short stops and that was it. And his time of coming back home, you know, from overseas was he'd been through so much, you know, after D-Day. And I didn't realize it but at that time I was, you know, still in college and so he did come -- he did get to come home, he was the second man in his outfit for battle fatigue that got to come back and so he did --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, tell us a little bit about his military history. Got in at 18 years old, got some quick training, and put him in 82nd --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, he was --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and he was gone.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He was gone, that's right and he was in the D-Day, you know.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, he parachuted into Normandy on D-Day --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes, and that was the night before --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- which was 82nd --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- yeah, the 82nd Airborne Division, he was in the 508th division at that time, had several of them, and the 101st, you know, and them. And then he made it -- like I say, he made it through that, and then they shipped him on up to, you know, the parts of France there and, you know, they were all involved. And then he was sent up to, let's see, it was Belgium Bulge, I guess.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yeah, one of the places, or Holland, when he jumped in Holland there and then Naymegan, I know that that's where he -- he took that -- one of the -- you know, they were trying to hold that bridge there, and so he took out one of those big tankers I guess, you know, by himself with, you know, and just to help hold that bridge. And that's where most of his guys were just annihilated, I mean, they were just wiped out. And so, there was no one to write up for him, you know. He should have gotten a Congressional Medal of Honor because he was -- but he did come out with the Silver Star and --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: He was awarded the Silver Star.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- and the Bronze -- three Bronzes and --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Purple Heart.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yeah, Purple Heart. And then -- and that's the reason why I wrote on that little page I gave you there. I wanted to get the rest of his -- you know, those countries over there had honored our 82nd Airborne fellows but he had been flown back up home because of battle fatigue and stuff so that he missed those ceremonies over there when they had them to give them their ribbons because he wanted my son to be able to wear them on his uniform, which he could, he said, but -- and I do have that list of the ribbons he should have gotten but I could not get through to -- past St. Louis, that they couldn't help me. They said I'd probably have to go through the different UN, you know, commission things through there to get to the different countries. And I want to do that yet, if I can, and I probably, you know, if I could get some help on that, why, I may try to do that because he deserves those. He has most of his other medals and things.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh. Well, that's quite an honor to receive the Silver Star --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, it is.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and the Purple Heart and to --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And do what he did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- and many other medals associated with winning the war.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: I know, yes, I know.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And jumping into Normandy on D-Day with the 82nd --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, I know.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Many of those men were killed.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Those fellows, they were all -- in fact, he had -- his leaders were all killed, you know, each time and they just practically wiped out the whole company so there was just a few of them left and he was just one of those fellows that was lucky. He was very -- well, he was a very logical person and his reactions were very, very quick, and that's what saved his life many times because he could act and think just like, you know, and he would think things out, you know. It's amazing but -- you know, I wish I could say the same for myself but, you know, I'm not that -- I wasn't -- but I'm sure that's what helped save his life many times.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, when did he get home and was discharged?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He was discharged in 1945 out of -- I'm trying to think here -- it was out of Alabama, I believe, is where he disembarked, out of Alabama. And yes, he came home and had to, you know, he wouldn't talk -- you know, they all had some rehab because it was hard for them to talk about the situation there for so long and, yet, he knew he had to get started in, you know, in his college because he had had some college courses, thank God, before he left, but he had to, you know, think about that, but he needed the time off just to get his mind back to, you know, thinking about going back to school and that sort of thing.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did he come back and go --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- so, you were a young girl, a college student at that time.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, and I was -- well, I was just -- yes, I was, I was still finishing up --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And so, did he start school?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: -- I was getting ready to start -- yes, I was getting ready to start my internship at the hospital there and, of course, that's when we were -- so, he had waited three months, and then he started up to K State, Kansas State, and under the GI Bill, which, you know, most of them did. And then we were -- I started my internship in '47, the fall of '47, and then I got through there in 1948 and then we were married, you know, there in '48 and he was still in college, you know, still in school.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So when did he finish his schooling?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He finished his school there in nineteen -- let's see, I think it was '50 -- '51 or '50 -- yeah, well, in '51 was the '51 flood. He was still going. In fact, he was marooned up there at K State (chuckles) you know, because of the '51 flood.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: He couldn't get home to see you.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He couldn't get home and so he says, I'm not going to stay up -- because we were just newlyweds, it was really -- no, it wasn't funny but, you know, it was a horrible flood.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Oh, that he was living there and you were here?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, you see, we had to live apart while --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: But you had been married.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes, we were married, yes, but, you know, I had to be here because I was working, I had my first job, and actually, you know, it was -- so anyway, he says, I'm going to get -- I'm going to get home. Because, you know, all the communications was knocked out and everything. So, what does he do? He wades on out and comes on out, you know, being an ol' paratrooper, he wasn't going to stay there (chuckles). So, he took this kid -- was a freshman -- and I guess he was his roommate or something, I don't know, anyway, he says, this young big old farmer kid from out in western Kansas, he says, If you're Al, I'm going with you -- he says -- I'm going with -- he says -- I'm not going to stay here either. And so, he was bringing this kid home and he was -- and he went clear up to Atchison. They had to go clear around because all the roads, you know, a lot were under and everything and so they hitchhiked. He hitchhiked. Got a ride, some guy was going to Atchison. He says, I don't care where you're going -- he says -- I'm going out there. So, then they hitchhiked from Atchison on in to Kansas City here. And I tell you, that was really something. So he made it home. I mean, he got out of there. But it was one of those things. But I guess it was '52 when he got through or around them, I'm not sure. I should remember all this stuff, but anyway.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You had an apartment in Kansas City?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, I didn't have. I tell you what, I stayed with my folks.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Because -- and then we had our first little -- this was while he was over there at school, we had bought this little old house that was in the 1903 flood that was sitting out there on the other side of Vera Lakes (ph) and it was our house and it went through the flood, clear through the 12-foot ceilings and, of course, we lost all our wedding presents and stuff, you know, but anyway, we were okay. We were young and we could make it back. And, of course, his mother lived real close and, of course, she lost everything which was bad for the older people, you know. But, anyway, yeah, we thought that was just great. You know, I was a city girl. I wasn't raised on a farm or anything so I wasn't used to outdoor plumbing and all this stuff (laughing) so I had to learn a lot (laughing). It was kind of fun.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: But you did it.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, yes, went through that too. But, you know, we were happy, we were in love and, you know, we were young, and we could take it (chuckles).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What did your husband, Al, do in his career?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: What did he do? He was a registered civil engineer and surveyor in three states here, Kansas, Missouri, and also Texas, he got that, and I think he was -- yeah, I was going to say -- and mostly here in Kansas and Missouri. And he worked for the cities and he was a director of public works and he was all around about civil engineering and all parts of it too, and hydraulics and stuff like this, and he worked for several big engineering firms first and then kind of went with the cities and the state. We were both ends -- I think both ends of our states, Kansas and Missouri, which kind of was an experience because for me especially because I was born and raised, you know, in a little round world all of my own here, you know, and wasn't used to the moving around but we did.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, how long were you married when he passed away?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: We would have been married 52 years when he passed away.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And when did he pass away?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He passed away in July of 2000.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: July of 2000.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, you had a good, long married life, not as long as you'd like, but it was a good long one, starting when you were both very young --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- he was first back out of the service and you still going to college at that time.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes, I was -- yes, I was.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And so, well, tell me about your family.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Tell me about your children.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, my children? Yes, I had -- my daughter was our firstborn. I was -- we were married about three -- let's see, three or three-and-a-half years when she was born, we waited, and so I was lucky to have her. I have an Rh factor which at the time they didn't have the Rh factor program at the -- the immunization that they give now, and so my second pregnancy was like 17 months later. My first child was, of course, it didn't affect the first child.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What's her name?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Alice.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Alice Charmaine [ph] Ruttinger.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, go ahead and tell me about Alice and then we'll go --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Alice, yes, grew up here in the Johnson County schools and then when we went to -- when my husband was in public works at Great Bend, she went to school out there and graduated. Went to K State. She started out at KU and that was in the '60s and that was when they had all the hippy problems, and, you know, they almost closed KU down. So, my father -- or my husband said, Well, she's not going to stay up there -- and, you know, because we had -- she lived kind of a closed life with us, we kind of watched her. And so, anyway, he said, I'm going to be sure she goes to K State. So, we transferred her out there. She was on the honor roll at KU also but she graduated on the honor -- with honors at K State and she entered medical school here in Kansas City, Missouri, and she's went through medical school here and she became -- she went into internal medicine, she's certified -- board certified, registered in that. She went to -- she gave -- I was really proud of her because she became Physician of the Year for the national Indian group in Oklahoma. She worked there because, you know, to pay back her tuition, part of it, for two years and the Nations, the Indian Nations there gave her two pow wows as Physician of the Year because she went beyond the cause and took care of a lot of the Indian women and, you know, helped them and they loved her so much -- and I'm not saying that because she's my daughter but she earned it, you know what I mean? She did it.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Where does she live now?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: She's in Sedalia, Missouri.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: She's in Sedalia, Missouri. Does she have children?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: She has children, my two grandsons.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And their names are?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: My names -- their names are James Alan Stevens Gought [ph] and Joshua Andrew Stevens Gought [ph] and they're the only two I have.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How old are James and Joshua?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: James just turned 17; and Joshua just turned -- he's going to be -- he's 13, he's going to be 14 here in September, the last part of September.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, you have a daughter. Then how about other members of your family?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay. Now, I lost the twins, they were the second pregnancy and they were quadriplegics that was due to the Rh factor so we had, you know, quite a thing to bear in our lives but I thank God I had, you know, a career at the time because we had -- you know, would have been a disaster for finances because the price and the training and stuff. We tried everything with them -- cost very much and we had to put them in a private institution at the last. But they were beautiful girls and they served their purpose according to the CEO at the home. They were in a Christian home.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: How old were they when they passed away?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, Annette was 14; and Carol died on her 21st birthday.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: H'm.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: They were beautiful children. When you looked at them you couldn't see there was anything wrong but they had been brain damaged from this Rh. They weren't transfused like they should have been. It was one of those unknown Rh problems at the time because we had very few. And then, I wasn't supposed to have any more children, naturally, but seven years later here comes a little blessed mistake, and that was my son. But I always wished for a son and so we were -- had a wonderful pediatrician and we were able to save him transfusing him, and he's also a doctor.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: What is his name?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: His name is Albert Clark Ruttinger.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Named after his father.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes. He was named after his father except for the middle initial, so we go by A -- he would by go by A. Clark. So, we'd go by "Clark," you know, his middle -- and he -- so he's had quite a, you know, quite a career too. Because, naturally, he followed in our footsteps. He graduated from K State with his honors and he went through the university Kansas City Medical School here also. And then he joined the U.S. Reserves now, because, you know, to play his part -- and back. And, of course, he became an officer in the Reserves. And then he was, of course, married the first time in I think it was 1987 I think is when he -- but, anyway, he took his residency. He went into just family medicine, he took a lot of that in Tulsa, Oklahoma, and down in Oklahoma City. And then he left -- let's see, he left Oklahoma and went to Arizona, and this is where he started his training in geriatrics there at the University of Tucson. He was in the -- he had to be transferred, of course, his reserve unit which he transferred out there. And he was into two months of his residency there at the University of Tucson in geriatrics when they called him up for Desert Storm. So he -- oh, bless you, honey, do you want a Kleenex (chuckles)? And he went to Desert Storm, of course, and paid his dues there. He was in the largest hospital unit on the front lines in Desert Storm. He said, Mom -- the first thing he said -- Mom, it's just like M.A.S.H. on television (laughing) -- and of course, you know, he was in the rough out there in those tents. And he says, Would you send me one of those inflatable mattresses -- he said. And we had to send him all kinds of things, you know, I mean, kid, just doing that. And he says, Oh, it's heck -- he says -- you know it's (chuckles)-- but anyway, we did, and we sent him cameras and oh, gosh, everything. Well, some of the stuff he got -- and, of course, you know, my family all pitched in, you know, my sisters and all, they all wanted to send stuff to him. And we's hoping that most of it would get to him but a lot of didn't because, you know, there was a lot of pilfering there and everything. But anyway, he come back from that and he was -- he had just finished his geriatrics residency there and came -- had his first job up to Phoenix. He went in with a group of specialists who was in a clinic there called Casablanca, the clinic. And was in, oh, nearly a year down the road, almost a year with them, when the unit that he got into out there in Arizona, the medical unit was a small unit was the only one they had at the time and he was made -- they made him commander of that group, you know, he took over as commander, which was quite a prestige for him and good background and training. And then, there was a unit -- medical unit in California that needed -- that was short -- they was calling for guys to come over to relieve the doctors there in Bosnia. Only thing available at that time -- he was single at that time and so they saw this family medicine, they wanted one of each specialty, plus a family practice or family medicine guy. And so, Clark's name came up, off he goes. I mean, he had to go to (chuckles) -- and I was really worried then because, you know, I thought, oh, gee, if he gets over -- because, you know, that was a mess. And so, he got -- he went. And I said, Well, let me know where you land -- because I said -- you know, it's really dangerous over there at that time. And so, he was lucky enough to get to go to the -- there was an old Hitler's [ph] hospital that had been converted and the U.S. took it over at the edge of Germany right there and they were taking the boys back from the front lines there and also the single families, you know, the families that were there of the boys. And so, that's where he went, he landed there, and took -- relieved those doctors because they had had no relief whatsoever. And, I mean, you know, we don't realize, I guess just what the heartaches are and the hard work and stuff because -- and they just -- They were so tickled to get him and all -- the German doctors and the other doctors, the foreign doctors over there said, Well, you know -- and I guess he was really, you know, shaping them up in a lot of ways over there (laughing) because, you know, I guess they thought the American boys didn't know much but I guess he showed them up. But they didn't want him to leave. They said, Oh, you know, we need you over here (chuckles). But he says, Oh, no.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, he got back.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He got back.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: He's in private practice out in Scottsdale.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes. And then he went on up to -- then when he came back, of course, he left that group because in the meantime -- that was a sad thing -- they had cut their salaries and all these young kids had come in, you know, the young doctors. The old doctors had theirs, you know, they made theirs. But these young kids, oh, it was pitiful. So, he left them and so then he got -- he had finished his geriatrics, he had taken his boards and everything. So he went up to -- he had a position offered to him at the clinic up at Sun City West, so that's where he went and the clinics up there then, some of those closed. And so, he said, Well, you know, if I'm going to have -- and he was -- one doctor had taken him in but he was trying to get him out of the red, which he did, but he lost thousands of dollars because he really took care for him. And he said, Well, if I'm going to have to work, you know, around the clock -- which they did if you're a good doctor -- and he says -- I'm going to go in solo -- he says -- I'm going to go in by myself. And that's what he did and that's where he is now. The only problem is, you know, he'd been in the Reserves for 20 years and he was commander of his medical group for Tucson for five-and-a-half years. He was only supposed to be there three years but they talked him into it. And so, finally he's out of that but what's happened is he didn't -- they wanted him to be as a consultant, they wanted him to stay in, you know, after -- and that's when he should have gotten out. But now, you know, he's sitting there. Now we're fighting another battle -- because I don't know, you know, he's more than doubled his practice, he's done real well. I went out there his first year when he opened up here in '01 in January and kind of did what I could, you know, just to be there. And, you know, he's working with a lot of -- 95 percent of the geriatrics patients are senior citizens which I could relate to because I am one, you know, and I worked in the Allied health field for a number of years so I really, you know, felt like I could do a little bit of good to get him started, you know, and -- which I did and I enjoyed it and I had a lot of fun with the patients too because, you know, they knew that I was just like them (chuckles).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, he still has the --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: He still has the private practice and he was doing so great, never had to advertise. He more than doubled his practice and then, of course, this year now with this situation like we had. Of course, President Bush says the war is over, you know, with Iraq but still, all in all, they're still saying that he may have to put in his 100 days. And, of course, this would ruin him because, you know, he can't find a doctor to replace him, you see. And he's there up there in a real, you know, place where there's just, you know, 95 percent of the people are -- and then he has families too, you know, whole families he treats.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: He doesn't have any children.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, he doesn't.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Okay. So, you have two wonderful children, both of whom are doctors.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: One lives close by in Sedalia.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Couple hours away.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then, she has your two grandsons who are --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Right, two grandsons.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- at a wonderful age.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, that's terrific.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, you did a marvelous job of going right to work in the summertime in the munitions plant doing your part at the -- I guess we'd called it at the powder plant over in De Soto.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, a lot of them referred to it like that, you know, (chuckles).

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And then, you had a wonderful career, a wonderful marriage with a --

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Oh, he was great.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: -- man who did a wonderful job in the war and was highly decorated, and then you have a wonderful family. Why don't you -- I know you have picture of your wedding.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Shortly after your wedding when you and Al were married. Let's take a look at that.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Okay (indicating.)

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: So, here we have shot of Al and Helen (indicating).

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: And the little ring bearer.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: And the little ring bearer, can't see him right now.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: No, that's okay.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: That is a gorgeous picture of a wonderful couple married 52 years before Al passed away. Two wonderful children, both physicians, and the two grandchildren, great kids. So, Helen, how do you feel about one's duty, one's obligation to serve a country in times of need?

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, I feel that we all are good Americans and our forefathers fought for this country so that we could be here and have the freedom we have so I really feel that I'd really like to be dedicated to all of our Veterans that have served and all of our veteran organizations and I support them dearly even to this day as much I can financially. And I hope to volunteer very shortly again at the VA hospital and probably the DAV and some of our other veterans' organizations. I feel that we all need to never forget what freedom really means because we tend to think of, you know, other countries being, you know, so far advanced from us, but really, you've got to look at what we have and we've made and what they've sacrificed for us, we know that we're still the greatest country.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: Well, Helen, I want to thank you very much for this interview and thank you for what you did for our country back when you were able.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Well, thank you, sir.

sp.speaker: Gary Swanson
sp.p: You're welcome.

sp.speaker: Helen A. Lucas Ruttinger
sp.p: Appreciate it.
